newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's Suharto seen as unlikely to step down.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Suharto seen as unlikely to step down.

text.p: President Suharto's advancing age is unlikely to stop his nomination for a seventh five-year term in office next year, political and diplomatic analysts said on Wednesday.
They were reacting to a comment by the 75-year-old president that people wishing to nominate him before a meeting of the People's Consultative Assembly (MPR) in 1998 should take account of his age.
"Please take my age into account because I will be 77," the chairman of the Indonesian National Youth Committee quoted the president as saying after they met on Tuesday.
The rupiah gave some ground against the dollar in early trading on Wednesday as some offshore dealers sold the Indonesian currency following the president's comment.

But local dealers dismissed suggestions that Suharto might step down and said offshore players were just using it as an excuse to trade. Spot rupiah was at 2,399 to the dollar and there was no noticable reaction on the stock exchange.

Market analysts said both the foreign exchange and equities markets had largely discounted the effects of May 29 general elections, which the ruling Golkar is expected to win comfortably, and next year's presidential poll.
"I think he (Suharto) is being coy," Juwono Sudarsono, professor of political science at the University of Indonesia, told Reuters.

"He's made a number of references to that effect over the past 15 years, every time before the session of the MPR. In fact he's said, 'if you don't want me, you just have to make sure the MPR withdraws my mandate', and I think this is one of those occasions," Sudarsono added.

Senior diplomatic sources said there was no indication that Suharto, whose 30-year rule has brought stability and economic growth to the sprawling archipelago of 200 million people, intended to step aside. He was still very much in control.
"There are no second thoughts about going for another term," one diplomat quoted well-placed Indonesians as saying.
"Some people might raise this question (of his age) and he was just getting it out of the way," he said.

Suharto took over power from Indonesia's late founding president Sukarno in March 1966 amid rising public discontent following an abortive coup bid the previous year widely blamed on the now-banned Indonesian Communist Party (PKI).

The People's Consultative Assembly, whose members had been appointed by Suharto, stripped Sukarno of all his titles, including president for life, in March 1967 and elected Suharto acting president. He was elected president the following year.

A key question mark still hangs over the vice-presidency, with the possibility that Suharto's deputy might inherit the ruler's mantle given the president's age and intermittent concern over his health.

Try Sutrisno is currently vice-president, but Suharto has never kept the same deputy for more than one term. While a number of names have been mentioned, there has been no consensus so far on a replacement.
